records.title: Front Hub Bearing Assembly Failure Causing ABS Activation, Noise, and Wheel Play
records.description: Front wheel hub bearing assemblies on Sierra 1500 trucks commonly wear out, especially on 4WD models and trucks used with larger tires or in rough conditions. Owners report humming or growling that changes with speed, looseness in the front wheel, and in some cases ABS warnings or low-speed ABS activation because the wheel speed sensor is integrated into the hub. This is a frequent repair item across both GMT800 and GMT900 generations.
records.solution: Diagnosis involves checking for wheel play with the tire off the ground, listening for bearing noise during road tests, and comparing wheel speed sensor data if ABS symptoms are present. Repair is replacement of the affected hub assembly, and many owners replace both sides if mileage is high. Corrosion at the sensor mounting surfaces and wiring damage should also be addressed to prevent repeat ABS issues.

records.title: Fuel Level Sensor Failure Causing Erratic or Inoperative Gas Gauge
records.description: A very common GMT800 complaint is sulfur contamination and wear of the fuel level sensor contacts inside the tank module, causing the gauge to read empty, full, or fluctuate unpredictably. Owners often see a low-fuel warning with plenty of fuel in the tank or watch the gauge drop suddenly while driving. GM issued service information and special coverage on many trucks for this exact condition.
records.solution: Confirm the issue by comparing scan-tool fuel level data and observing whether the sender reading jumps erratically. The usual repair is replacement of the fuel level sensor or, more commonly, the entire fuel pump module assembly because of labor overlap and the age of the pump. Connector condition and ground integrity should also be checked during service.

records.title: Fuel Pump Module Failure Causing No-Start or Stalling
records.description: A common GMT800 Sierra problem is failure of the in-tank fuel pump module, often from worn pump motors or failed level-sender/module electronics. Owners report long crank, hard starting, loss of power under load, or sudden stall/no-start conditions, especially as mileage climbs. This issue is widely documented in owner forums and complaint databases across 4.3L, 4.8L, 5.3L, and 6.0L trucks.
records.solution: Diagnosis usually starts with checking fuel pressure at the rail and verifying pump prime at key-on. Low or unstable pressure, especially after sitting, points to a weak pump or failing module. Repair is replacement of the complete fuel pump module and, ideally, the fuel filter on applicable years; corroded electrical connectors at the tank should also be inspected and replaced if heat-damaged.

records.title: Knock Sensor Water Intrusion Under Intake Causing Check Engine Light and Reduced Performance
records.description: The 4.8L, 5.3L, and 6.0L Vortec engines used in early GMT800 Sierra trucks place the knock sensors in wells beneath the intake manifold, where water can collect and corrode the sensors or harness. Owners frequently report recurring check-engine lights, timing retard, and reduced power, especially after washing the engine bay or driving in wet conditions. GM issued service information addressing knock sensor corrosion and revised sealing practices.
records.solution: Diagnosis involves scanning for knock sensor circuit codes, checking freeze-frame data, and inspecting the sensor wells and sub-harness under the intake for moisture or corrosion. Proper repair is replacement of both knock sensors and the harness, cleaning the valley area, and resealing the intake and sensor openings with the updated grommets/sealant procedure to prevent repeat failures.

records.title: Power Door Lock Actuator Failure Causing Intermittent or Inoperative Locking
records.description: GMT900 Sierra trucks are well known for failing door lock actuators, often starting with one door that unlocks weakly or only works intermittently before additional doors fail. Owners report the key fob cycling the locks while one or more doors remain stuck, requiring manual operation from inside. The issue is heavily documented across GM full-size truck forums and complaint records.
records.solution: Diagnosis involves confirming power and ground at the latch/actuator assembly and ruling out broken door-jamb wiring or BCM command issues. The usual fix is replacement of the failed actuator or latch-actuator assembly in the affected door, followed by checking all doors because multiple actuators often fail within a similar time period.

records.title: Rusting Brake Lines Leading to Fluid Loss and Sudden Brake Failure
records.description: Corrosion of steel brake lines is a major safety issue on older Sierra 1500 trucks, especially in salt-belt states. Owners report the brake pedal suddenly dropping to the floor when a rusted line bursts during normal braking, often near the ABS module or along the frame rails. The problem is heavily documented in NHTSA complaints and repair forums for GMT800 trucks and related GM full-size pickups.
records.solution: Inspect all hard brake lines from the master cylinder/ABS module to the rear axle and front calipers, paying close attention to flaking rust and wet spots. Spot repairs may buy time, but many owners end up replacing the full line set with pre-bent stainless or coated steel lines because multiple sections are usually compromised. After replacement, the system must be properly bled, including ABS bleed procedures when needed.

records.title: Stepper Motor Instrument Cluster Failure Causing Inaccurate Gauges
records.description: 2003-2007 Classic-era Sierra trucks are well known for instrument cluster gauge failures caused by defective stepper motors and, in some cases, backlighting issues. Speedometer, tachometer, oil pressure, fuel, voltage, and coolant gauges can stick, read wildly high or low, or stop moving entirely. The problem became widespread enough that GM issued a special coverage adjustment on many trucks and SUVs using the same cluster design.
records.solution: Verify actual vehicle data with a scan tool or GPS speed app to confirm the cluster is inaccurate rather than the sending unit. Repair is typically cluster removal and professional rebuild with updated stepper motors and bulbs, or replacement with a remanufactured unit programmed for the vehicle. If only one gauge is wrong, the whole cluster is still usually rebuilt because the remaining motors often fail later.

The problem is widely discussed in owner communities for GMT900 GM trucks and appears repeatedly in complaint databases.
records.solution: Inspect for cracks around the passenger-side airbag opening, center speaker area, and defrost vent corners. Repair options include replacing the dash pad, installing a molded dash cap, or using plastic repair methods for minor cracks; replacement is the most durable but also the most labor-intensive and expensive option.

records.title: 4.3L V6 Intake Manifold Gasket Leak
records.description: Same intake gasket issue as the S-10 platform. The 4.3L Vortec V6 intake gaskets fail from heat cycling.
records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the intake manifold-to-head sealing area for external coolant seepage; on the 4.3L Vortec, leaks commonly occur at the lower intake manifold gaskets and can also show up as unexplained coolant loss or overheating. Repair requires removing the upper plenum and lower intake manifold, cleaning the sealing surfaces, and installing the updated metal/rubber intake manifold gasket set with new bolts if specified, then refilling and properly bleeding the cooling system; many technicians also change the thermostat and coolant during the job. If coolant contamination is found in the oil, change the oil and filter immediately after repair. Typical repair cost is about $700-$1,300 depending on labor rates and whether related items like hoses, thermostat, or distributor components are replaced.

records.title: In-Tank Fuel Pump Failure
records.description: Same fuel pump failure issues as the S-10. The in-tank pump fails from heat and debris.
records.solution: Confirm low fuel pressure before replacing parts by checking pressure at the Schrader valve on the fuel rail; CPI/Vortec-equipped 4.3L trucks are especially sensitive and typically need about 60-66 psi to start and run correctly, while weak pressure, intermittent drop-out, or excessive current draw points to a failing in-tank pump. Inspect the fuel pump relay, fuse, ground at the frame, and the pump electrical connector for heat damage, then replace the complete in-tank fuel pump module/strainer and install a new fuel filter at the same time; on many Sonomas the tank must be lowered, though removing the bed can also improve access on some configurations. Use a quality Delco or Delphi module rather than a pump-only repair, and clean out any tank debris to prevent repeat failure. Typical repair cost is about $450-$900 parts and labor depending on engine, cab/bed configuration, and whether the sending unit harness also needs replacement.

records.title: 5.7L Vortec Intake Manifold Gasket and CPI Issues
records.description: The GMC Suburban shares the same 5.7L Vortec intake gasket and spider injector issues as the C/K 1500. The larger vehicle runs hotter, which can accelerate gasket degradation.
records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect for external seepage at the lower intake manifold gasket, then scan fuel trims/misfire data and remove the upper plenum to check the Central Port Injection (CPI) spider for fuel leakage or sticking poppets. Repair typically involves replacing the lower intake manifold gaskets with the updated metal/rubber design, changing coolant and engine oil if contaminated, and torquing the intake in sequence to spec; if the CPI unit is leaking or causing hard starts/rough idle, replace it with the updated MFI spider assembly. Parts are usually about $120-$250 for intake gasket sets and $250-$450 for the injector assembly, with total repair costs commonly running $900-$1,800 depending on labor rates and whether both problems are addressed together.
symptoms: Coolant leak
Rough idle
Hard starting
Fuel smell

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 93V016 - Suburban Transmission Vent

records.title: Fuel Pump Failure in Large Tank
records.description: The in-tank fuel pump works harder due to the Suburban's large fuel tank (42 gallons) and fails prematurely. The pump draws more current to push fuel the longer distance to the engine, leading to burnout.
records.solution: Replace fuel pump module assembly (Delphi FG0100). The large tank makes this job more involved - support the tank properly during removal. Replace the fuel filter (frame-mounted) at the same time.
symptoms: Loss of power at highway speed
Extended cranking to start
Engine cuts out under acceleration
Whining from rear of vehicle

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 95V026 - Suburban Transmission Case

records.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure
records.description: The Suburban's HVAC system uses multiple electric blend door actuators that fail, causing one side of the cabin to blow hot while the other blows cold. The actuators' internal gears strip, and the clicking sound they make when failing is unmistakable.
records.solution: Replace the failed blend door actuator. There are three or four actuators depending on the climate control option — identify the failed one by the clicking sound location. Actuators are behind the dash but the driver-side one can be accessed from below.
symptoms: Clicking from behind dashboard
One side blows hot, other blows cold
Temperature stuck on hot or cold
Defrost not working
Clicking sound on startup or mode change
Air only comes from one vent position

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 95V139 - Suburban Shift Cable

records.title: Rear AC Evaporator Core and Line Leaks
records.description: The GMC Suburban (and Chevrolet Suburban/Tahoe/Yukon) with rear AC systems develop leaks in the rear evaporator core and the aluminum rear AC lines that run along the passenger-side frame rail. The lines corrode under the securing straps from road salt and moisture. The rear drain tube also clogs, causing musty odors inside the cabin. Repair is costly because the rear AC system is difficult to access.
records.solution: Confirm the leak by recovering the refrigerant, pulling the system into vacuum, and pressure-testing with dry nitrogen and UV dye or an electronic leak detector at the rear evaporator case and the aluminum lines running along the passenger-side frame rail, especially under the retaining clamps. Replace any corroded rear lines and, if leaking, the rear evaporator core and O-rings, then flush debris, evacuate the system, recharge to factory specification, and clear the rear evaporator drain tube to stop water intrusion and mildew odor. Many owners in rust-belt areas choose a rear A/C line delete or block-off kit if rear cooling is not needed, which is cheaper than full line replacement. Typical cost is about $400-$900 for line repair/delete, or roughly $1,200-$2,000+ if the rear evaporator core and interior trim access labor are required.
symptoms: Rear AC blows warm air
Musty or mildew smell from rear vents
Refrigerant loss requiring frequent recharges
Water leaking inside cargo area
Visible corrosion on rear AC lines along frame rail

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 96V057 - Suburban Throttle Cable

records.title: Rear HVAC Blower Motor and Heater Core Failure
records.description: The rear heating and A/C system suffers from blower motor failure and rear heater core leaks. The rear heater core is located under the rear cargo area and is susceptible to coolant corrosion.
records.solution: Replace rear blower motor (VDO PM3542) and/or rear heater core. The rear heater core requires removal of rear cargo panels for access. Flush the cooling system and use proper coolant mix to prevent future corrosion.
symptoms: No heat or A/C in rear
Coolant smell in cargo area
Wet carpet in rear
Rear blower motor doesn't work

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 98V033 - Suburban Rotor/Hub

records.title: 1.5L Turbo PCV System Failure and Coolant/Oil Intrusion
records.description: The 2018+ Terrain with the 1.5L turbocharged engine (LFV/LYX) experiences PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) diaphragm failure inside the valve cover. The integrated PCV diaphragm tears, causing excessive crankcase pressure that forces oil into the intake manifold and intercooler. Symptoms include oily residue around the air intake and intercooler outlet pipe. In severe cases, excessive crankcase pressure also causes coolant intrusion into the combustion chamber. GM issued TSB PIT5697 for this issue. This is the same problem affecting the Chevrolet Equinox 1.5T of the same era.
records.solution: Replace valve cover assembly with updated GM part (GM 12690058) which includes the revised PCV diaphragm. Clean intercooler and intake manifold of oil contamination. Check for coolant consumption alongside oil intrusion. Inspect air-to-water intercooler for coolant contamination — replacement if contaminated (GM 84446987).
symptoms: Oil residue in intercooler outlet pipe or air intake
Blue/white smoke from exhaust
Coolant level dropping with no visible external leak
Rough idle after cold start
Check engine light (boost, MAF, or misfire codes)
Oil smell from engine bay

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 09V489 - Center-Control Module and Defroster Recall

records.title: 2.4L I4 Excessive Oil Consumption and Piston Ring Failure
records.description: The 2.4L LEA and LE9 four-cylinder engines in 2010-2017 Terrain are among the most reported excessive oil consumption issues in GM's lineup. Many owners consume 1 quart of oil every 1,000-2,000 miles. The root cause is inadequate piston ring tension combined with piston ring land fractures that allow oil to bypass rings into the combustion chamber. The problem was subject to class action lawsuits and GM Customer Satisfaction Programs. Burned oil causes spark plug fouling, catalytic converter damage, and oil pressure warnings. This is the same issue affecting the Chevy Equinox with the same engine.
records.solution: GM formal oil consumption test (PIP4656D): measure consumption over 3,000 miles. If over 1 qt/2,000 miles, piston ring replacement authorized under warranty/extended warranty. Short-term: use Dexos1 Gen 2 full synthetic and check oil every 1,000 miles. Replaced engines available from GM on documented repeat failures.
symptoms: Oil level dropping 1+ quart every 1,000-2,000 miles
Blue smoke on acceleration or on startup
Spark plug fouling (oil on electrode)
Oil pressure warning light
Catalytic converter damage from oil burning
Engine running rough (fouled plugs)

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 10V623 - Front Seat-Belt Buckle Anchor Recall

records.title: Ecotec 2.4L Timing Chain and Tensioner Failure
records.description: The GM Ecotec 2.4L in the 2010-2014 Terrain has the same timing chain stretch and tensioner failure as the Equinox and Malibu. GM Special Coverage Adjustment SCA 12313C covers some vehicles. The 2010-2011 models are worst affected. Improperly hardened piston rings on 2010-2013 models cause excessive oil burning, which leads to low oil and accelerated timing chain wear. 2015+ models received revised internal components.
symptoms: Rattling noise on cold start
Check engine light with P0016 or P0017
Rough idle and misfires
Excessive oil consumption (1 qt per 1000 miles)
Loss of power and poor acceleration
Engine stalling

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 14V447 - Power-Seat Height-Adjuster Bolt Recall

records.title: Electric Power Steering Sticking / Increased Steering Effort
records.description: First-generation Terrains (shared with the Chevy Equinox) develop a "sticky" power-steering condition where the wheel binds on-center - most often after long straight-highway driving - and requires noticeably higher effort to turn. NHTSA investigated roughly 781,000 2010-2012 units. GM traced it to increased friction in the steering gear and addressed it via a service bulletin/special coverage rather than a full recall; NHTSA closed the probe in 2022 with no recall.
records.solution: GM Service Bulletin (PI0814-series, 2014) directs technicians to replace the original steering gear (rack) with a redesigned unit; repairs were covered at no cost under special coverage. Out-of-warranty repair is replacement of the steering gear assembly.
symptoms: Steering wheel feels sticky on-center
Increased effort to turn
Momentary steering bind after long straight driving
Vehicle wanders or drifts

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 15V666 - Front Side-Airbag Inflator Recall

records.title: Electronic Shifter Fault - Vehicle Stuck in Park / "Shift to Park" Message
records.description: Second-generation Terrains with the electronic precision (push-button/monostable) shifter throw a persistent "Shift to Park" warning and refuse to shift out of (or fully into) park even when correctly positioned. GM traced it to build-up/contamination on the Park switch contacts in the transmission control (shifter) assembly, causing high resistance so the BCM cannot electronically confirm the Park position. It can strand the vehicle and, in many cases, keeps the ignition from turning off (stuck in Accessory).
records.solution: GM issued field actions ranging from an ECM/BCM software update to a shifter wire-harness/jumper change and ultimately replacement of the shifter control (transmission control button) assembly. Dealers first clear the fault; recurring cases get a new shifter cartridge or full center-console shifter unit.
symptoms: "Shift to Park" message won't clear
Cannot shift out of park
Cannot turn engine off (stuck in Accessory)
Intermittent no-shift condition
Warning chime persists

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 16V502 - Replacement Park-Lock Lever Recall

records.title: Engine-Driven Brake Vacuum Pump Failure - Sudden Loss of Power Brake Assist (Hard Pedal)
records.description: On second-generation Terrains (2018-2022) with the 1.5L LYX and 2.0L LTG turbo engines, the camshaft-driven mechanical vacuum pump that supplies the brake booster can fail suddenly and without warning. When it fails, drivers lose power brake assist and the pedal becomes hard as a rock, requiring dramatically increased effort to stop and greatly increasing crash risk. In severe cases pump internals disintegrate and send metal debris into the engine oil, contaminating internal components and turning a brake repair into a costly engine job. The defect is the subject of a February 18, 2026 proposed federal class-action (Thieme, Gill, Morley v. General Motors, LLC, E.D. Michigan) covering 2018-2022 Equinox/Terrain and 2016-2020 Buick Envision; the suit alleges GM knew of the issue as early as a March 2017 stop-delivery order. No recall has been issued as of mid-2026.
records.solution: Replace the failed camshaft-driven vacuum pump (and the brake booster if it was damaged). If the pump disintegrated, an oil-system flush and inspection for metal contamination is required; catastrophic cases need internal engine repair. With no recall issued, repairs are typically owner-paid unless covered by powertrain warranty or resolved through the pending class action.
symptoms: Brake pedal suddenly hard/stiff and difficult to press
Loss of power brake assist
Longer stopping distances
Whining or knocking noise from front of engine
Metal shavings in engine oil in severe cases

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 16V582 - Windshield-Wiper Module Recall

records.title: High-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure Causing Engine Stall (Recall)
records.description: On 1.5L turbo Terrains, a component inside the high-pressure fuel pump can fracture prematurely, generating metallic debris that migrates through the fuel line and blocks the injector inlets, starving the engine of fuel and causing sudden stalling and loss of power while driving - a crash risk. GM recall N222372310 (NHTSA 23V-013) covers the 2022 Terrain; broader inadequate-fuel-flow actions span the 2021-2023 range.
records.solution: Under recall, dealers replace the fuel pump module and update the engine control software free of charge. Owners should verify their VIN against open recalls via NHTSA or a GMC dealer.
symptoms: Sudden engine stall while driving
Loss of power/propulsion
Hard starting or no-start
Check engine light
Rough running

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 23V013 - Inadequate Fuel-Pump Flow Recall

records.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure (Clicking Noise, No Temperature Control)
records.description: The HVAC blend/mode-door actuators fail as their internal plastic gears strip, producing a repetitive clicking or knocking sound from behind the dash and causing loss of temperature or airflow control. On dual-zone systems one side commonly blows hot while the other blows cold, or the system sticks on one temperature. A click/pop typically means a stripped gear requiring replacement.
records.solution: Replace the failed blend/mode-door actuator (OEM/ACDelco recommended to avoid repeat aftermarket failures) and recalibrate with a scan tool after installation. The temperature (blend) actuator is the most common failure; mode/recirc actuators can also fail.
symptoms: Repetitive clicking/knocking behind dash
One side hot, other side cold
Stuck on cold or hot air
Temperature setting has no effect
No airflow mode change

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 17V516 - Right Front Intermediate Driveshaft Recall

records.title: IntelliLink Infotainment Freezing/Rebooting and Backup Camera Black Screen
records.description: The IntelliLink/MyLink touchscreen freezes and spontaneously reboots, losing control of radio, climate, navigation and Bluetooth, and often displays a black screen or a frozen backup-camera image. During a reboot, phone calls drop and the rear camera can go dark while in reverse - a visibility concern. Root causes include software glitches, outdated firmware, and occasionally loose display/camera wiring.
records.solution: Start with a software/firmware update at the dealer and a system reset (Home + Fast Forward held ~10s, or Return to Factory Settings). Persistent cases require reseating/repairing loose harness connectors or replacing the radio/display module or backup camera.
symptoms: Touchscreen freezes or reboots
Black/blank infotainment screen
Backup camera not working or shows frozen image
Lost radio/Bluetooth/nav
Dropped phone calls on reboot

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 18V340 - Airbag Control-Module Power-Down Recall

records.title: Start/Stop Transmission Accumulator Endcap Missing Bolts - Fluid Leak & Loss of Propulsion (Recall)
records.description: On second-gen Terrains, the automatic transmission's start/stop accumulator endcap may have been assembled with missing bolts, allowing transmission fluid to leak. The leak can progress to loss of propulsion and, if fluid contacts an ignition source, a fire risk. GM recall N202313440 (NHTSA 20V-668) covers certain 2018-2020 Terrain and Equinox units - more than 217,000 vehicles in the US and Canada.
records.solution: Under recall (began December 2020), dealers inspect the start/stop transmission accumulator and replace it if any bolts are missing, free of charge. Owners should check their VIN for this open recall.
symptoms: Transmission fluid leak / puddle under vehicle
Loss of propulsion
Slipping or no drive
Burning smell
Low transmission fluid

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 20V668 - Start/Stop Accumulator Endcap Recall

records.title: Throttle Body / Throttle Position Sensor Failure - 'Reduced Engine Power' Warning
records.description: First-generation Terrains (2010-2017) are prone to a sudden 'Reduced Engine Power' warning caused by a failing electronic throttle body. Carbon and grime build up inside the bore and the internal throttle position sensor (TPS) fails or reads erratically, causing the ECM to enter a limp/reduced-power mode that limits the vehicle to very low speed. This is a widely reported failure on the naturally aspirated 2.4L four-cylinder and 3.6L V6 engines and frequently appears alongside a 'Service StabiliTrak' message. The most commonly cited trouble code is P2135 (throttle/pedal position sensor voltage correlation). No NHTSA recall covers the throttle body; it is addressed through non-recall repair.
records.solution: Clean the throttle body if carbon buildup is the cause; if the throttle position sensor has failed the electronic throttle body assembly is replaced as a unit and the idle/throttle relearn procedure is performed.
symptoms: 'Reduced Engine Power' message on dash
Sudden loss of acceleration / limp mode
Check engine light
'Service StabiliTrak' message
Rough idle or stalling

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 18V358 - High-Pressure Fuel-Pump Mounting Recall

records.title: 6T40/6T45 6-Speed Transmission Shudder and Harsh Shifts
records.description: The 2010-2017 Terrain uses the GM 6T40 (2.4L) and 6T45 (V6) 6-speed automatic transmissions, both of which suffer from torque converter shudder, harsh shifts, and solenoid failures. The shudder occurs at light throttle between 30-50 mph when the torque converter clutch locks up. Solenoid pack wear causes P0756, P0751, and P0776 transmission fault codes. The transmission is sensitive to fluid condition — the 6T40/6T45 was originally filled with Dexron VI, but older Dexron VI degrades faster than newer formulations.
records.solution: Full fluid exchange with Dexron VI (ACDelco 10-9243 or equivalent). TCM calibration update. Solenoid pack replacement (GM 24272814) if codes present. Valve body replacement for internal failures. Fluid service every 40,000 miles recommended for stop-and-go use.
symptoms: Shudder at light throttle 30-50 mph
Harsh 1-2 or 2-3 upshift
Hesitation or lurch when pulling away from a stop
Transmission fault codes P0756, P0751, P0776
Check engine light
Delayed engagement from Park to Drive when hot

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 18V576 - Rear Brake-Caliper Piston Recall

records.title: Water Pump Failure and Coolant Leak
records.description: The engine-driven water pump develops bearing/impeller wear or seal leaks, allowing coolant to weep (often visible as dried Dex-Cool on the timing-chain cover or flung from the pump pulley) and eventually causing overheating. On both the 2.4L Ecotec and 3.6L V6, the pump is timing-chain-cover-mounted, making replacement labor-intensive and comparatively expensive. Neglecting a leaking pump can damage timing components.
records.solution: Replace the water pump (OEM/ACDelco) along with the coolant and inspect the thermostat and hoses. Given the timing-cover location, professional replacement is recommended; refill and bleed the cooling system afterward.
symptoms: Coolant leak / puddle under front of vehicle
Engine overheating
Low coolant warning
Whining or grinding from water pump
Sweet coolant smell

records.title: 10L80 10-Speed Transmission Harsh Shifting, Shudder and Rear-Wheel Lock-Up
records.description: The 10L80/10L90 ten-speed automatic exhibits harsh 1-2 upshifts when cold, steady-speed shudder around 40-70 mph, and a lag into Drive/Reverse that ends with a jolt. The failure point is valve-body wear and internal pressure leaks. In the worst case a transmission control-valve defect can cause a momentary rear-wheel lock-up; GM issued a large recall covering over 460,000 2020-2022 Silverado/Sierra/Tahoe/Suburban/Yukon/Escalade for this control valve. Multiple class-action suits have been filed and symptoms often surface between 40,000-60,000 miles.
records.solution: For the safety recall, dealers inspect and replace the transmission control valve (valve body) as required. For general shudder/harsh shifts, GM service procedures call for a transmission fluid flush with the correct Mobil 1 DEXRON-ULV (low-viscosity) fluid and, where wear is present, valve-body replacement; reprogramming the TCM with the latest calibration addresses many harsh-shift complaints. Confirm the transmission recall status by VIN before paying out of pocket.
symptoms: Harsh or clunky 1-2 upshift, especially when cold
Shudder/vibration at steady 40-70 mph cruise
Delayed engagement into Drive or Reverse with a jolt
Slipping or flaring between gears
Momentary rear-wheel lock-up (recall condition)

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 24V797 - Diesel Transmission Control-Valve Recall

records.title: 5.3L V8 Excessive Oil Consumption (AFM Oil Spray / Piston Rings)
records.description: The Active Fuel Management (AFM) 5.3L V8 burns oil at an abnormal rate, frequently a quart every 1,500-2,500 miles. The AFM pressure-relief valve in the valley sprays oil onto the cylinder walls when cylinders deactivate; combined with low-tension/coking piston rings and an oil-drawing PCV design, oil is drawn into the combustion chamber and burned. This is distinct from AFM lifter collapse - here the engine consumes oil, fouls plugs, and can run low enough to trigger misfires and low-oil warnings. A class-action settlement covered the LC9 5.3L piston-ring defect.
records.solution: GM's oil-consumption TSB fix installs updated pistons and rings and an AFM oil-deflector/shield in the valley. Common owner remedies: replace the PCV/updated valve covers, keep the oil topped up, and install an AFM/DOD delete or a catch can to stop the oil spray before ring damage occurs. If rings are already coked, a piston/ring job (or short block) is required. Verify oil-consumption class-action eligibility for affected VINs.
symptoms: Burning ~1 quart per 1,500-2,500 miles
Low oil level / low oil pressure warning
Blue smoke on startup or acceleration
Fouled spark plugs and rough idle / misfire
Engine sludge / carbon buildup

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 00V343 - Rear Wheelhouse Plug Exhaust-Gas Recall

records.title: 6.2L L87 V8 Rod Bearing Failure and Loss of Propulsion
records.description: The 6.2L L87 V8 in 2021-2024 Yukons can suffer catastrophic engine failure from connecting-rod bearing damage. GM's own teardown analysis (Recall 25V-274 / N252494001) identified two supplier root causes: machining sediment left on the connecting rods and in the crankshaft oil galleries, and out-of-specification crankshaft dimensions/surface finish. The bearings spin and the engine can knock, seize, or throw a rod through the block, causing sudden loss of propulsion at speed. NHTSA logged thousands of loss-of-propulsion allegations and opened an investigation into post-recall failures. Roughly 82,000 Yukons are within the affected population.
records.solution: Under Recall 25V-274 GM inspects the engine; failed units get a full engine replacement (some receive GM remanufactured long blocks), and engines that pass inspection get a revised oil-fill spec switching from 0W-20 to thicker 0W-40 (GM dexos1 Gen 3), a new oil-fill cap, and a service-procedure update. Out of warranty, a rod-knock engine typically needs a complete engine or long-block replacement. Owners should have the recall performed at a GMC dealer at no charge and monitor for knocking or oil-pressure warnings.
symptoms: Deep knocking or rod-knock noise from the engine
Sudden loss of power or stalling while driving
Metallic debris in the oil
Low oil pressure warning
Engine seizure / no-start

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 25V274 - 6.2L Connecting-Rod and Crankshaft Recall

records.title: 8L90 8-Speed Torque Converter Shudder
records.description: The 8L90 8-speed automatic transmission in 2015-2020 Yukon and Yukon XL suffers from widespread torque converter lock-up clutch shudder at light throttle between 25-50 mph. The clutch friction material degrades and contaminates the transmission fluid, causing the shudder to worsen over time. GM extended warranty coverage to 6 years/100,000 miles under Customer Satisfaction Program 18302. The fluid fix (Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP, GM 19417577) resolves early-stage cases; advanced cases require torque converter replacement. This is the same issue affecting all K2XX platform full-size GM SUVs and trucks.
records.solution: Full transmission fluid exchange with Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP (GM 19417577). Check Customer Satisfaction Program 18302 coverage. Torque converter replacement (GM 24288828) for persistent cases. Complete flush requires 17-20 quarts — ensure dealer uses full volume per TSB 18-NA-355.
symptoms: Shudder or vibration at light throttle 25-50 mph
Feels like driving on rumble strips at highway speed
Harsh 1-2 or 2-3 shifts
Momentary slip when accelerating from a stop
Shudder disappears at full throttle

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 14V152 - Transmission Oil-Cooler Line Recall

records.title: AFM/DOD Lifter Collapse and Valvetrain Failure
records.description: The GMC Yukon 5.3L (L83, LC9, LMG) and 6.2L (L94, L86) V8 engines use Active Fuel Management (AFM) cylinder deactivation. The special collapsible AFM lifters on cylinders 1, 4, 6, and 7 fail prematurely, causing misfires, engine ticking, rough idle, and potential catastrophic damage. This is the single most reported mechanical failure on GMT900 (2007-2014) and K2XX (2015-2020) Yukon models. GM issued TSB 18-NA-077 acknowledging the issue. Yukon models used as daily drivers with lots of highway cruising (where AFM activates most) are most susceptible. The VLOM (Valve Lifter Oil Manifold) must also be replaced as it controls oil flow to AFM lifters.
records.solution: Replace all 16 lifters, VLOM (GM 12639516), and inspect camshaft lobes. AFM delete kit (Texas Speed or BTR) permanently eliminates the system. Range Technology AFM Disabler RA003B prevents AFM activation as a preventive measure. Change oil every 5,000 miles with Dexos1 Gen 2 full synthetic to protect lifters.
symptoms: Misfire codes P0300, P0301, P0304, P0306, P0307
Engine tick or tap at idle that worsens with load
Rough idle or engine vibration
Check engine light
Reduced engine power / limp mode
Metal debris in oil (confirmed on drain plug inspection)
Vibration between 30-55 mph during V4 deactivation mode

citations.title: NHTSA Campaign 11V007 - Rear-Axle Cross-Pin Recall

records.title: Autoride Air Suspension Compressor and Air Bag Failure
records.description: Yukon and Yukon XL models equipped with Autoride (RPO Z55) or electronic suspension feature rear air springs and a compressor that commonly fail between 80,000-130,000 miles. The air spring bags crack from age and temperature cycling, causing the rear of the vehicle to sag overnight. The compressor burns out from running continuously to compensate for air spring leaks. Replacing OEM components and having them fail again is common — many owners convert to passive coil springs. Same system as Chevy Tahoe/Suburban and Escalade.
records.solution: Replace air springs and compressor (Arnott P-2793 compressor). Or install Arnott C-2835 / Strutmasters conversion kit to permanently eliminate air suspension with coil springs plus electronic bypass module. Conversion kits cost $400-700 and eliminate future air suspension failures.
symptoms: Rear of vehicle sagging overnight or after sitting
Compressor running continuously
SERVICE RIDE CONTROL or AIR SUSPENSION message
Bouncy or harsh ride quality
One corner lower than others
Compressor fails to raise vehicle

records.title: Automatic 4WD Transfer Case Position Sensor / Encoder Motor Failure
records.description: On Autotrac electronic-shift 4WD Yukons the transfer-case encoder motor and its position sensor/selector switch fail, so the module can no longer confirm the range. The dash 4WD buttons flash, the truck won't shift between 2HI/4HI/4LO or gets stuck in one range, the Service 4WD light comes on, and codes such as C038D 'Range Actuator Position Not Learned' are stored. Worn encoder-motor contacts and corroded connector pins are typical causes.
records.solution: Diagnose whether the fault is the encoder motor, the position sensor/selector, or the transfer case control module. Common repairs: replace the transfer-case encoder/shift motor and the two/four-wheel-drive actuator position sensor (GM Genuine 84377721 / 84368196), and repin/repair the corroded connector. After replacement the actuator position must be relearned with a scan tool. Cleaning the dash 4WD switch contacts fixes some no-shift complaints.
symptoms: Flashing 4WD selector buttons
'Service 4WD' warning light
Won't shift between 2HI/4HI/4LO or stuck in range
Grinding/clicking from the transfer case during shift
Neutral indicator won't confirm

records.title: Brake Vacuum Pump Failure Causing Hard Brake Pedal
records.description: The engine-driven mechanical vacuum pump that supplies power-brake boost can lose output when debris and oil sludge build up on its internal filter screen. Reduced vacuum means the brake booster no longer assists as designed, so the pedal becomes hard and stopping distances increase. GM Recall 19V-645 covers roughly 3.4 million 2014-2018 full-size trucks and SUVs including the 2015-2018 Yukon; GM reported 113 crashes and 13 injuries tied to the defect.
records.solution: Under Recall 19V-645 dealers reprogram the electronic brake control module to increase hydraulic brake assist when vacuum drops (free of charge). If the vacuum pump itself has failed, it is replaced with an updated ACDelco unit. Watch for the 'Service Brake Assist' message; drivers who lose assist should press the pedal firmly with steady pressure and get the recall completed. Verify the recall is closed by VIN at a GMC dealer.
symptoms: Hard/stiff brake pedal requiring extra force
Increased stopping distance
'Service Brake Assist' warning message
Ticking noise from the engine bay
Vibrating brake pedal

records.title: Cracked Dashboard Over Airbag and Instrument Panel
records.description: The one-piece molded dash pad splits and cracks, most often along the seam above the passenger airbag and over the instrument cluster. Owners attribute it to GM's switch from a multi-piece to a one-piece design with insufficient relief points and over-tightened mounting bolts, combined with heat/UV aging. Beyond the cosmetic damage there is a safety concern that a cracked seam can affect passenger-airbag deployment. A multi-state class action was filed in 2018 (E.D. Michigan); NHTSA declined a formal recall.
records.solution: The permanent fix is replacing the upper dash pad/instrument-panel trim pad (dealer quotes commonly around $1,500-$1,800 installed). Budget alternatives include a molded ABS dash cap/overlay bonded over the cracked pad or a carpeted dash cover. Parking in shade and using a windshield sunshade slows further cracking. There is no factory recall, so repair is owner-paid unless covered by an extended warranty.
symptoms: Cracks radiating from the passenger airbag seam
Split in the dash over the instrument cluster
Sharp raised edges of vinyl/plastic
Rattles or squeaks from the loose dash pad

records.title: Engine Overheat/Fail-Safe Mode from Thermostat and Coolant Temp Sensor
records.description: A worn or leaking factory thermostat that stays open (plus a failing engine coolant temperature sensor) prevents the engine from reaching normal operating temperature. The ECM interprets the low/erratic reading as a sensor fault and enters a protective fail-safe mode: the electric cooling fans run at full speed continuously, the temperature gauge may drop to zero or read erratically, the A/C compressor may be disabled, and fuel economy suffers. It is a common and well-documented complaint across 2015-2019 5.3L/6.2L trucks and SUVs.
records.solution: Diagnose whether the thermostat is stuck open or the ECT sensor has drifted. The usual repair is replacing the integrated thermostat housing and the engine coolant temperature sensor (GM Genuine ECT sensor 12608814) together with fresh DEXCOOL. Clearing the codes and confirming the engine reaches ~210F resolves the fans-on-full and disabled-A/C behavior. Address it promptly because the fail-safe also cuts A/C and hurts mileage.
symptoms: Cooling fans running at full speed constantly
Temperature gauge reads zero or fluctuates
A/C compressor won't engage / no cold air
Engine slow to warm up in cold weather
Reduced fuel economy, check-engine light

records.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure (Clicking Behind Dash)
records.description: The small electric blend-door actuators that control temperature and air-flow direction strip their internal plastic gears, producing a repetitive tapping/clicking noise from behind the radio or glovebox and causing the HVAC to blow the wrong temperature (e.g., stuck cold on the passenger side) or fail to change modes. It is one of the most common comfort complaints on the GMT900 Yukon and often affects more than one of the several actuators over the vehicle's life.
records.solution: Replace the failed actuator with a GM Original Equipment ACDelco unit - the passenger temperature actuator is ACDelco 15-72971 (GM 89018365 / 52402588; aftermarket cross Dorman 604-106). Before buying parts, pull the HVAC fuse for ~60 seconds to force a recalibration in case the fault is only a stuck cal. After replacement, reconnect the battery and let the system self-calibrate. OEM/ACDelco parts are strongly recommended because cheap aftermarket actuators have a high early-failure rate on this platform.
symptoms: Repetitive clicking/tapping behind the dash or glovebox
One side blows hot while the other blows cold
Air won't switch between vents/floor/defrost
Temperature setting doesn't change actual output

records.title: Instrument Cluster Stepper Motor / Gauge Failure
records.description: The gauge cluster on 2003-2006 Yukons uses small stepper motors (the factory Switec/Juken X25.168-series) that wear out or jam. The speedometer, tachometer, fuel, or temperature needles twitch, flutter, stick, read wildly inaccurate, or peg at zero or maximum. A stuck or wrong speedometer is a safety and driveability concern and is one of the single most common electrical complaints on the GMT800 platform.
records.solution: Rebuild the cluster by replacing the failed stepper motors with updated X27.168 motors (a solder/DIY kit runs roughly $30-$60 plus new bulbs), or send the cluster to a specialist repair service (typically $120-$300 with a lifetime warranty). Full cluster replacement is possible but requires reprogramming the odometer/VIN, so a stepper-motor rebuild is the preferred, cheaper fix. Replacing all six motors at once is recommended since they fail in sequence.
symptoms: Speedometer or tach needle sticks, jumps, or reads wrong
Needles flutter or bounce erratically
Gauge pegged at zero or maximum
Fuel/temp gauge inaccurate
Needle stuck after key-off

records.title: Intermediate Steering Shaft Clunk / Pop
records.description: A hallmark GMT800 complaint: a clunk or knock felt in the steering wheel and column when turning at low speed or driving over small bumps and rough pavement. The intermediate steering shaft (I-shaft) splines wear and lose lubrication, so the shaft binds and then releases with an audible/tactile pop. It is a comfort/annoyance issue rather than a loss-of-control safety defect, but it is extremely common and frequently returns after temporary fixes.
records.solution: Temporary fix: lubricate the I-shaft with the GM Steering Column Intermediate Shaft Lubrication Kit (P/N 26098419). Permanent fix: replace the intermediate steering shaft with the updated non-serviceable unit (P/N 19153614) - note the newer design cannot and should not be greased. Confirm the clunk is the I-shaft (not the steering gear or a worn U-joint) before replacing.
symptoms: Clunk/knock felt in the steering wheel over bumps
Popping when turning at low speed
Notchy feel in the steering column
Noise worse on rough roads with steering input

records.title: MyLink / IntelliLink 8-Inch Touchscreen Failure
records.description: The 8-inch MyLink/IntelliLink infotainment touchscreen (RPO IO5/IO6) develops ghost touches where it presses buttons by itself, dead zones that stop responding, and delamination/bubbling where the digitizer separates from the LCD. Because so many K2XX Yukons share this radio, it is one of the most common infotainment failures on the platform, disabling climate, backup-camera overlays, and audio controls that are routed through the screen.
records.solution: The permanent fix is replacing the failing capacitive touchscreen/digitizer (common service part reference DJ080PA-01A for the 8-inch unit) or sending the HMI/radio control panel to a specialist for a screen/digitizer rebuild - typically far cheaper than a new GM radio. A software update from the dealer can clear intermittent freezes but does not fix a delaminated or ghost-touching panel. Confirm whether the unit is IO5 (no nav) or IO6 (nav) so the correct replacement is used.
symptoms: Ghost touches / screen presses by itself
Unresponsive areas of the touchscreen
Bubbling, haze, or delamination in the display
Screen freezes or reboots
Loss of climate/audio/camera controls routed through the screen

records.title: Power Running Board Motor Failure and Corrosion
records.description: The power retractable running boards available on 2015+ Yukon and Yukon XL are a common failure point. The electric motors and gearboxes corrode and seize, especially in salt-belt states. Boards get stuck in the out position (creating a road-clearance hazard and trip risk) or refuse to extend. The wiring harness connections at the running board motors corrode. GM has released multiple updated motor designs, but corrosion in the mechanical linkage pins also causes binding. Repair cost is $800-2,000 per side if both motors fail.
records.solution: Motor replacement (GM 84085689 updated motor). Lubricate pivot points and linkage pins with marine-grade grease annually. Dielectric grease on harness connectors. Some owners disable the system and lock boards in a fixed position to avoid ongoing failures.
symptoms: Running boards stuck in out position
Running boards not extending when door opens
Grinding or clicking noise when boards deploy
Service Running Boards message on DIC
Boards deploy on one side only
Boards extend but don't fully retract under the truck

records.title: Water Pump Weep-Hole Leak and Coolant Loss
records.description: The mechanical (belt-driven) water pump develops internal bearing and seal wear with age and mileage, then leaks coolant from the weep hole at the front-center of the engine. Left unaddressed the pump can drip DEXCOOL onto the ground, run the cooling system low, and cause overheating. It is a common wear item on the Gen IV/V small-block V8s used across the GMT900 and K2XX Yukon and typically shows up beyond ~90,000-120,000 miles.
records.solution: Replace the water pump (ACDelco Professional water pump for the applicable V8) with a new gasket, and refill with GM DEXCOOL. Because the serpentine belt, thermostat, and hoses are already accessed during the job, it is recommended to replace the thermostat and inspect the belt at the same time. Catch the weep-hole leak early to avoid an overheating event and possible head-gasket damage.
symptoms: Coolant puddle/drip at the front-center of the engine
Coolant seeping from the pump weep hole
Low coolant level / frequent top-offs
Overheating or rising temperature gauge
Whining or grinding from a failing pump bearing

records.title: Brake Line Corrosion and Failure (GMT900 Platform)
records.description: The 2007-2014 Yukon XL shares the GMT900 platform with the Suburban, Silverado, and Sierra, and suffers the same steel brake line corrosion issue in salt-belt states. Factory lines corrode externally and can rupture without warning. NHTSA Recall 17V-449 covers limited VINs. Full-size long-wheelbase vehicles like the Yukon XL have more linear feet of brake line exposed to road salt than shorter vehicles, making inspection and replacement especially important.
records.solution: Replace corroded lines with Dorman 919-149 stainless steel kit for long-wheelbase GMT900 (Suburban/Yukon XL). Annual brake line inspection in salt-belt states. Fluid flush every 3 years to prevent internal corrosion.

records.title: Cracked Exhaust Manifold Bolts / Manifold Leak (5.3L/6.2L V8) Causing Cold-Start Tick
records.description: Yukon XL V8 engines (notably 5.3L and 6.2L) can develop broken exhaust manifold bolts and/or warped manifolds, leading to an exhaust leak that is loudest on cold start. Owners describe a ticking sound that diminishes as the engine warms and the manifold expands. This is a well-documented GM truck/SUV issue in owner reports and service discussions for these engines.
records.solution: Replace broken manifold bolts/studs and install updated hardware; resurface or replace the exhaust manifold if warped. Inspect for missing bolt heads and use proper extraction methods; replace manifold gaskets if applicable for the engine/year.

Exhaust smell in engine bay
Soot marks near manifold flange
Noise decreases as engine warms

records.title: Dashboard Cracking and Warping from UV/Heat Exposure
records.description: The K2UC (2015-2020) generation Yukon XL dashboards develop cracks, warping, and delamination from UV exposure and heat cycling, particularly in southern states. Cracks typically originate near the defroster vents and passenger airbag seam and spread across the dash surface. The issue is covered under GM special coverage adjustment 14311 for some VINs, extending the warranty to 10 years. Beyond cosmetic concerns, severe cracking near the passenger airbag seam can affect proper airbag deployment.
records.solution: Check VIN eligibility for GM special coverage 14311 (free dashboard replacement at dealer, 10-year coverage). If not covered, dashboard replacement costs $800-2,000+ at a dealer. Aftermarket dashboard covers from DashMat or Coverlay are $150-300 alternatives that cover existing cracks. For a proper repair, the entire instrument panel must be removed (6-8 hours labor). Prevention: use a windshield sunshade and apply 303 Aerospace Protectant to the dash surface quarterly.
symptoms: Visible cracks spreading from defroster vent area
Dashboard surface warping or bubbling
Shiny or sticky texture on dashboard
Cracks near passenger airbag deployment seam
Rattling from loose dashboard pieces

records.title: Door Handle/Linkage Failure (Exterior Handle Pulls but Door Won’t Open)
records.description: Yukon XL owner reports frequently cite exterior door handles or internal linkage rods/clips failing, causing the handle to move without unlatching the door. This can occur on front or rear doors and may worsen in cold weather or after repeated use as plastic clips fatigue. The issue is widely documented in owner forums and NHTSA complaints for full-size GM SUVs/trucks of these generations.
records.solution: Remove the door panel and replace the failed handle assembly and/or linkage clips/rods; inspect latch operation and lubricate the latch mechanism. Use OEM replacement handle/linkage components matched to the door and model year.

Owners report sudden heavy steering and a warning message/chime.
records.solution: Perform the recall remedy/inspection and replace affected EPS components as directed by GM (commonly steering gear/EPS motor or related wiring/connectors depending on build). Confirm open recall status by VIN and complete dealer repair.

records.title: Rear Liftgate Support Strut Failure
records.description: The Yukon XL rear liftgate gas struts lose their charge and fail to hold the heavy liftgate open, typically between 3-5 years regardless of mileage. The oversized liftgate of the XL model is significantly heavier than the standard Yukon, putting more stress on the struts. A failing strut allows the liftgate to slowly drop or slam closed, posing a head injury risk. In cold weather, weak struts fail more noticeably due to gas contraction.
records.solution: Replace both liftgate support struts as a pair (never replace just one). Strongarm 6262 or Sachs SG330090 are popular OE-equivalent replacements. The replacement takes about 15 minutes with a trim removal tool to pop the ball socket clips. Ensure the new struts are rated for the correct force (the XL requires higher-force struts than the standard Yukon). Power liftgate models should have the motor assembly inspected simultaneously.
symptoms: Liftgate does not stay open fully
Liftgate slowly drops after opening
Liftgate slams closed unexpectedly
More noticeable in cold weather
Hissing sound from strut (gas leak)

records.title: Magnetic Ride Control (MRC) Shock/Strut Fluid Leak and 'Service Suspension System' Warnings
records.description: Yukon XL Denali and other trims equipped with Magnetic Ride Control can develop leaking dampers and internal failure, leading to degraded ride quality and suspension fault messages. Owner reports commonly describe bouncy/floaty ride, clunking over bumps, and repeated 'Service Suspension System' alerts as the shocks lose damping control. This is frequently documented in owner forums and NHTSA complaints for K2XX-era Yukon XL with MRC.
records.solution: Replace failed MRC shocks/struts (often in pairs on the same axle) and recalibrate/clear suspension codes. Use OEM MRC dampers (ACDelco/GM) matched to the vehicle’s RPO codes; inspect wiring/connectors at each damper for damage/corrosion.

records.title: Steering Column Lock Actuator Click and Binding
records.description: The electronic steering column lock (ESCL) actuator in 2015-2020 Yukon XL models develops a clicking, popping, or grinding noise when turning the steering wheel, particularly at startup. In some cases, the ESCL prevents the vehicle from starting entirely, displaying a "Steering Column Lock" message. GM issued TSB 16-NA-012 acknowledging the issue. The ESCL motor gear teeth strip or the position sensor misreads, causing the lock to partially engage or fail to release.
records.solution: Replace the electronic steering column lock actuator assembly (GM part 13501988). The replacement procedure requires disconnecting the battery, removing the lower steering column cover, and swapping the ESCL module. A Tech 2 or MDI scan tool relearn procedure must be performed after installation to program the new module to the BCM. Some owners have the ESCL permanently disabled via BCM programming at the dealer, though this may affect theft deterrent system operation.
symptoms: Clicking or popping noise from steering column on startup
Vehicle will not start — Steering Column Lock message
Grinding noise when turning the key or pressing start

Steering wheel feels temporarily locked after parking

records.title: Transmission Torque Converter Shudder (8L90/10L80)
records.description: The 8-speed (8L90) and 10-speed (10L80) automatic transmissions in the Yukon XL develop a torque converter clutch (TCC) shudder felt as a vibration or shake at light throttle between 25-50 mph. The shudder mimics driving over rumble strips. GM issued multiple TSBs (18-NA-355, 19-NA-193) and eventually reformulated the transmission fluid specification. The root cause is the TCC friction material interaction with the original Dexron HP fluid formulation.
records.solution: First-line fix: complete transmission fluid flush and fill with GM-approved Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP (Blue Label) — NOT the original red-label Dexron HP. This updated fluid resolves the shudder in approximately 80% of cases. If shudder returns within 30,000 miles of the fluid change, the torque converter requires replacement. Do NOT use aftermarket friction modifiers or additives — they void the GM powertrain warranty and can damage the transmission.
symptoms: Vibration or shudder at 25-50 mph under light throttle
Feels like driving over rumble strips
Shudder disappears under heavy acceleration
Vibration most noticeable in overdrive gears
Intermittent — may come and go

records.title: Transfer Case Fluid Leak from Output Shaft Seal
records.description: Four-wheel-drive Yukon XL models with the NP263 (NQH) and NP246 transfer cases develop fluid leaks from the front and rear output shaft seals. The leak typically starts as a slow weep and progresses to a steady drip, leaving ATF spots on the driveway. If left unaddressed, the transfer case runs low on fluid, causing internal damage to the chain, sprockets, and bearings. The rear output seal is the most common failure point.
records.solution: Replace the leaking output shaft seal(s). The rear seal can be replaced with the transfer case in the vehicle by removing the rear driveshaft and prying out the old seal. The front seal requires more disassembly. Use only genuine ACDelco seals (ACDelco 24232325) as aftermarket seals have a higher failure rate on this application. Refill with Dexron VI ATF to the proper level. Inspect the output shaft for scoring — a scored shaft will destroy the new seal quickly.
symptoms: ATF dripping from transfer case area
Transfer case fluid low at service intervals
Grinding or whining noise from transfer case
Difficulty engaging 4WD
Service 4WD message on dashboard

records.title: Front Hub Bearing and ABS Wheel Speed Sensor Corrosion Causing Unwanted ABS Activation
records.description: GMT800 SUVs commonly develop corrosion under the front wheel speed sensors or wear in the hub bearing assembly, which alters the low-speed wheel speed signal. The result is unexpected ABS activation at parking-lot speeds, longer stopping distances, and a pulsating brake pedal even on dry pavement. GM documented this condition in service bulletins, and owners frequently report replacing hub assemblies to cure it.
records.solution: Scan ABS wheel speed data during a low-speed stop and compare left and right front sensor readings. If one sensor drops out, inspect for rust buildup under the sensor or excessive hub play; cleaning the sensor mounting surface may help temporarily, but many vehicles need a complete front hub/bearing assembly with integrated sensor. records.title: Fuel Pump Module Failure Leading to No-Start or Intermittent Stalling
records.description: In-tank fuel pump module failure is a common GMT800 problem, especially as mileage climbs or when vehicles are frequently run near empty. The issue is well represented in owner reports and repair histories across 5.3L, 6.0L, and 8.1L applications.
records.solution: Verify fuel pressure at the rail and monitor pressure drop during key-on and cranking. If pressure is low or intermittent, replace the fuel pump module and inspect the electrical connector for heat damage; replacing the fuel filter at the same time is standard practice. On rusty vehicles, many owners choose to cut an access panel under the rear cargo area, though tank removal remains the factory method.

records.title: Intermediate Steering Shaft Clunk and Binding Over Bumps or During Turns
records.description: A very common GMT800 complaint is a clunk, knock, or slight bind felt through the steering wheel due to wear in the intermediate steering shaft. Owners often notice it at low speeds over small bumps, during parking maneuvers, or when transitioning on and off the brake. GM issued multiple service bulletins and revised shaft/lubrication procedures for this condition.
records.solution: Differentiate the noise from front suspension or steering gear play by checking the shaft for telescoping looseness and reproducing the clunk with the vehicle stationary. Depending on condition, the shaft can sometimes be lubricated per GM procedure, but replacement with the updated intermediate shaft is the more durable fix. After repair, verify steering wheel centering and absence of other front-end looseness.

noise during parking lot turns

records.title: Knock Sensor Water Intrusion Under Intake Causing Check Engine Light
records.description: The 4.8L, 5.3L, and 6.0L Vortec engines used in this generation commonly develop knock sensor faults because moisture collects in the valley beneath the intake manifold. Corrosion at the sensors or harness causes persistent P0327/P0332 codes, reduced spark advance, and occasional drivability complaints. This is a well-known GMT800 issue documented in GM service bulletins and owner forums.
records.solution: Scan for knock sensor codes, remove the intake manifold, and inspect both sensors, the sub-harness, and the rubber grommet seals. Replace both knock sensors and the harness together, clean the valley thoroughly, and reseal the sensor wells/grommets to prevent future water intrusion. Many technicians also verify no coolant leaks or cowl water leaks are contributing.
symptoms: check engine light
reduced power or sluggish acceleration
poor fuel economy
intermittent spark knock code
recurring P0327 or P0332 after rain or washing
